title: Ọjà: E-commerce Backend
summary: The backend for an Aba-made leather goods brand: a versioned REST API for products, carts, orders and payments, with a small storefront and admin built on top to prove it works.
tech: PostgreSQL on Neon (plain SQL, no ORM)
body:
Ọjà is the backend for a leather brand selling shoes, bags, belts and sandals from Ariaria market in Aba. Until Day 19, my pages called Server Actions directly. Today I built something other apps could use: a versioned REST API at `/api/v1`, documented on its own `/docs` page generated from an OpenAPI document. The storefront and admin on top use the same service layer, so the rules are identical whether you click a button or send a request.

Customers browse with filters, search and sort, keep a cart, apply coupons, choose a delivery state and pay through Paystack in test mode. Staff manage products, stock and orders. Admins manage coupons, delivery fees, users, API keys and the webhook log. A demo mode gives each visitor their own private customer account in one click, while the staff and admin views are read-only.

**What I learned:**

- Splitting the code into three layers (SQL, business rules, thin transport) keeps the website and the API from disagreeing with each other.
- Idempotency keys stop a double tap or a bad network from creating two orders.
- Cursor pagination stays fast on deep pages and doesn’t skip or repeat rows, unlike OFFSET.
- A single table of allowed order status moves is easier to trust than checks scattered across the code.
- Stock is taken with a guarded update inside one transaction, so it can’t go below zero even when two buyers race for the last item.
- A webhook has to verify its HMAC signature before anything is read, and the amount must match the order.
- Returning 404 instead of 403 for someone else’s order doesn’t reveal whether it exists.
- Running EXPLAIN on real queries showed two weak spots (a rare size and colour combination with a price sort, and full-text search at small scale), which I wrote up honestly in the README.
